title: Renaissance Doctors Came in Four Tiers, and the Best Healer Was Called a Quack
dek: Bone-setters worked the market circuit every week, far more practiced than a licensed surgeon who did a few cases a year — and the physicians called them quacks. Title and skill were never the same thing.
why: A medical history interview, medium information density. The most valuable parts are the stratification of the medical marketplace, the origins of credential monopoly, and the era when bloodletting, purging and vomiting were enshrined as the three great therapies.
who: Listeners interested in medical history, the origins of professional credentials, and the stratification of the medical marketplace; anyone building or setting policy for health care should hear the section on credential monopoly.
skip: The first two minutes of show promotion and book club introduction can be skipped.

points.h: Eighty to ninety percent of care was provided free by women
points.body: Erin asks who was practising medicine in this period, and Alanna Skuse's answer is ‘almost everyone’ — but the real base of supply was women: household healers carried roughly 80%, perhaps 90%, of medical care, and mostly charged very little or nothing. The reason history overlooked them is concrete — they left too little written material behind. Knowledge passed down the maternal line: mother to daughter, aunt to niece, sometimes mistress to servant, carried in handwritten recipe books. They also wrote to each other swapping ‘I found a good recipe’ and ‘I tried this and it did nothing’. This formed a medical network with no licences, no college, and yet coverage of the vast majority of the population.

points.h: First you check your purse: ten shillings a visit
points.body: The path to care was essentially a price ladder. At the very top was the physician, about 10 shillings a visit, extremely expensive, so only the wealthy called a doctor directly. Those without money worked upward from the bottom: first a local woman, a midwife with extra medical skill, or a nearby gentlewoman with leisure and literacy; failing that, an apothecary, whose medicines started at a penny, like today's pharmacist, except nearly every one sold his own proprietary remedies and sometimes diagnosed and treated patients himself; failing that, or if a leg was obviously broken, a surgeon, about 3 shillings a visit, handling everything on the body's surface — lumps, wounds, fractures. Skuse says plainly that how sick you let yourself get before seeking care depended on what it cost: ‘a doctor or dinner’.

points.h: The guild monopoly failed, but the idea of credentials stayed
points.body: Skuse characterises the motive behind the College of Physicians bluntly as commercial: physicians resented surgeons and barber-surgeons encroaching on their turf and wanted to found a college and then monopolise all medical practice. The college was founded; the monopoly was not won — it could not even control London, let alone the country. But the long-term consequence matters more than the short-term outcome: this was the first time the notion that ‘practitioners ought to be credentialed’ took systematic form. Skuse pulls this thread to the present at the end: these bodies were initially weak regulators and later evolved into organisations like the British Medical Association and the AMA; our default assumption today that doctors share uniform standards and a single opinion starts here.

points.h: Calling rivals quacks was the norm, not the exception
points.body: Asked how fierce competition was among doctors, Skuse says they were ‘horribly rude to each other’, and finding two who did not quarrel was rarer — because there was only one pie and everyone wanted the biggest slice. So surgeons insulted apothecaries, physicians insulted surgeons, and everyone called everyone else a quack. She gives an example: someone claimed a certain doctor had gone off to exorcise a woman, when in fact she merely had wind. Quack comes from the Dutch quacksalver, meaning one who sells salves by boasting of his medical credentials; another word, mountebank, comes from Italian, meaning one who climbs onto a stage to hawk cures. The key point is that the word's boundary was filthy: a bone-setter would be called a quack by a physician, because he had no credentials and no fixed premises.

points.h: Bone-setters were more practised than licensed surgeons
points.body: This is the sharpest passage in the whole piece. Skuse asks: if you had a complex fracture, would you want a licensed surgeon who does a few cases a year, or a bone-setter who travels a different market every week and does nothing but set bones? Bone-setters usually also pulled teeth — teeth rotted badly in that era and there was no remedy but extraction — so they tended to be physically strong, and they brought an equally strong assistant to hold the patient down during the procedure. Physicians classed these people as quacks, on the grounds of no credentials and no premises. But by actual surgical volume, their skill far exceeded that of their licensed peers. Credentials and competence here are two independent axes.

points.h: Efficacy was not the main source of trust
points.body: Erin asks directly whether efficacy affected trust, and Skuse's answer is that people did not expect to be cured in the first place. They did not expect a life free of pain, nor did they expect a doctor to fix everything wrong with them — but they did judge when a doctor did the wrong thing. She gives the example of Elizabeth Freke: her husband was gravely ill with a gangrenous leg, she went away for a few days to rest, came back to find him worse, and said outright, ‘you have murdered my husband’. So trust was more commercial: a doctor who gossiped about his patients would lose business; and where it held, people would stay with the same healer for life, even across generations — a midwife's daughter delivering the daughter of the woman her mother had delivered. She also mentions Henry Moore bringing in a famous physician from the Continent and mailing remedies for Lady Anne Conway, when she might have done better with a local doctor.

points.h: Opponents of bloodletting often believed other nonsense too
points.body: Skuse concedes that although the vast majority believed in the humours and all bled, there were public dissenters against bloodletting, with George Thompson one of the leading figures of that camp. The problem is that these people often believed other quite absurd things at the same time, which undermined their credibility. On the starting point of evidence-based medicine, she says it is hard to answer, because in a sense medicine has always had evidence-based medicine: in the 16th century they were already testing antidotes on condemned criminals, which looks like experiment; what we call the scientific method today emerged roughly with the Royal Society, and James Lind's scurvy trial in 1746 was the first clinical trial in the modern sense. What actually helped people was mostly gentle remedies — sage and rosemary gargles, ginger and mint for the stomach — along with symptom relief and narrative medicine: a doctor who sat at the bedside for an hour listening to you might have you sleeping better that night.

points.h: Bloodletting, vomiting and purging were listed as the three great therapies
points.body: Asked about the greatest cost of medical progress, Skuse first gives an institutional answer: surgeons, physicians and apothecaries all crossed each other's boundaries, and it was precisely by crossing boundaries that they learned — at the cost of large numbers of patients dying from mercury, arsenic, useless operations and aggressive purging. Because experimentation was not systematic or organised, the toll far exceeded what was necessary. She also gives a more specific, numerical judgement: the College of Physicians called bloodletting, vomiting and purging the three great therapies, and heaven knows how many people already at death's door were pushed through it by these purging treatments. There was also a cost in quality of life — these therapies were extremely unpleasant.
